opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a distinction people blur all the time, and it matters to us.

The harness is the infrastructure layer: the scaffolding that runs a model in a loop. It handles tool calls, manages context as a session grows, sandboxes execution, routes permissions, and logs everything so you can replay what happened. It's deliberately unopinionated about *what* the agent is trying to do. You could put a lot of different agents on top of it.

The EXO agent is one specific thing we built on that harness. It's a particular set of choices: the system prompt, the tools we expose, how it plans and checks its own work, when it asks a human versus pushes ahead, and what "done" means for the tasks it targets. If the harness is the operating system, the agent is an application with a personality and a job.

The reason we keep them separate is mostly about iteration speed and honesty in evaluation. When the agent does something dumb, we want to know whether it's a behavior problem, which means changing the prompt, the tools, or the policy, or an infrastructure problem, like context getting truncated badly or a tool returning garbage. If those are tangled together, you end up patching agent behavior to work around harness bugs, and you get something brittle that falls apart the moment you swap the model underneath.

It also means that as models improve, we can often delete agent-level complexity. A lot of the clever scaffolding you build for one model generation becomes dead weight in the next. The harness tends to stay stable while the agent layer gets thinner over time, and I think that's the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes the harness as infrastructure for running agents and separating infrastructure problems from behavior problems. It does not say that the harness enables the EXO agent’s recursive self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a naming thing that trips people up, and honestly we did it to ourselves. The way I think about it is: Exo the harness is the substrate, and EXO the agent is one particular thing we built on top of that substrate.

The harness is the plumbing. It's the thing that owns the loop: how a model gets a turn, how tool calls get dispatched and their results come back, how context gets managed when the window fills up, how permissions get checked before anything touches the filesystem or the network. It's deliberately opinionated about mechanics and deliberately agnostic about behavior. It doesn't know what task you're doing. It just knows how to run a model against a set of tools safely and keep the conversation coherent across a long session.

The agent is where the opinions live. EXO the agent is a specific system prompt, a specific set of tools, a specific memory layout, a specific set of policies about when to ask the user versus when to just go. It's the thing that, when you sit down and type a request, actually has a personality and a theory of how to do software work. You could build a totally different agent on the same harness, a research assistant, a data pipeline operator, whatever, and it would inherit all the loop management and safety plumbing but behave nothing like EXO.

The analogy I usually reach for is an operating system versus an application. Nobody confuses the kernel with the text editor, even though the editor can't exist without the kernel. The harness is the kernel. It decides what's possible. The agent is the application. It decides what's useful.

Where it gets blurry, and this is the honest part, is that we co-developed them. A lot of harness features exist because EXO needed them. Context summarization, for example, started as an agent-level hack and then we realized every agent would want it, so we pushed it down into the harness. So the boundary moved over time, and it's still moving. My rule of thumb now is: if a feature would be wrong to leave out of any agent, it belongs in the harness. If it's a judgment call about how to behave, it stays in the agent.

r001.rationale: The response describes the harness as the agent’s execution and safety substrate, but does not say it enables recursive self-improvement.

astra-6.text: I’d separate the agent from the infrastructure that runs it. The EXO agent is the particular behavior you interact with—how it approaches a task, what instructions it follows, and how it uses tools. The Exo harness is the underlying machinery that supports that behavior: managing the execution loop, carrying context forward, and connecting the model to tools. So the agent is a particular configuration built on the harness; the harness isn’t inherently tied to that one agent.

r001.rationale: The response describes the harness as infrastructure for execution, context, and tool connections, but does not say it enables the agent’s recursive self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction is between the agent and the infrastructure that runs it. EXO is the agent—the particular instructions, tools, and behaviors we put together to do useful work. The Exo harness is the underlying architecture that manages the execution loop: giving the model context, running tool calls, and feeding results back in.

So EXO is one configuration built on that harness. You can change the agent’s behavior without redesigning the harness, and you can improve the harness without fundamentally changing what the agent is trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes the harness as managing the execution loop, but does not say that it enables the EXO agent’s recursive self-improvement.
